\chapter{A Gift and a Feast}
\label{ch:hi-a-gift-and-a-feast}
\hlchaptermodality{57}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things that go with thanks in Hindi.}

Complete HI-C57-sweetness and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tohfā]{\hi{तोहफ़ा} (tohfā) — a present}

\label{lesson:HI-C57-present}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did the last two words of the chapter before mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{तोहफ़ा}}
\textbf{\hi{तोहफ़ा}} (\emph{tohfā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a present\textquotedblright{}.

An Arabic word, \emph{tuḥfa}, 'a gift, a rarity', arriving through Persian on the same road as \hi{दुकान} in the chapter before.

It carries a shade the English word does not: a \emph{tuḥfa} is a gift that is choice, something a little rarer than what the occasion required. That shade is faint in modern Hindi but it has not gone.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things that travel with thanks.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tohfā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tohfā}, offered with both hands
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{तोहफ़ा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a present\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dāvat]{\hi{दावत} (dāvat) — a feast, an invitation}

\label{lesson:HI-C57-feast}



\begin{quote}
What did the word before this one mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{दावत}}
\textbf{\hi{दावत}} (\emph{dāvat}) — \textquotedblleft{}a feast, an invitation\textquotedblright{}.

From Arabic \ar{دعوة} (\emph{daʿwa}), 'a call, a summons, an invitation', on the root \emph{d-ʿ-w}, 'to call'.

The meaning slid from the invitation to the meal you were invited to, which is a short slide and a common one. In Hindi \hi{दावत} can still be either — the calling or the eating — and the sentence decides which.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second of five, and a word that means both the calling and the meal.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dāvat}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dāvat}, and the \emph{tohfā} you bring to it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{दावत} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a feast, an invitation\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[thālī]{\hi{थाली} (thālī) — a metal platter}

\label{lesson:HI-C57-platter}



\begin{quote}
Name the 2 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{थाली}}
\textbf{\hi{थाली}} (\emph{thālī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a metal platter\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{स्थाली} (\emph{sthālī}), a cooking pot or dish. The initial \emph{sth-} cluster lost its \emph{s}, the same simplification you watched in \hi{कंधा}.

A \hi{थाली} is not a plate in the English sense but the round metal tray a whole meal is laid out on at once, small bowls and all — which is why the word names a way of eating and not just an object.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third of five, and the thing the \hi{दावत} arrives on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{thālī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{thālī}, and on it the \emph{dāl} and the \emph{chāval}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{थाली} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a metal platter\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khushbū]{\hi{ख़ुशबू} (khushbū) — fragrance}

\label{lesson:HI-C57-fragrance}



\begin{quote}
Name the 3 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{ख़ुशबू}}
\textbf{\hi{ख़ुशबू}} (\emph{khushbū}) — \textquotedblleft{}fragrance\textquotedblright{}.

Two Persian pieces, and you already own one of them: \emph{khush}, 'pleasant', is the \emph{khush-} inside \hi{ख़ुशी}, from the first time you were pleased to meet someone. \emph{bū} is 'smell'. \hi{ख़ुशबू} is a pleasant smell, said in the plainest way available.

Persian builds a great many words like this, and Hindi took the habit along with the words. Once you can hear the seam in the middle, a whole shelf of vocabulary stops being arbitrary.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fourth of five, and the first word you have been able to take apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{khushbū}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{khushbū}, and hear \hi{ख़ुशी} in its first half
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{ख़ुशबू} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}fragrance\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[miṭhās]{\hi{मिठास} (miṭhās) — sweetness}

\label{lesson:HI-C57-sweetness}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{मिठास}}
\textbf{\hi{मिठास}} (\emph{miṭhās}) — \textquotedblleft{}sweetness\textquotedblright{}.

Built on \hi{मीठा} (\emph{mīṭhā}), 'sweet', from Sanskrit \hi{मिष्ट} (\emph{miṣṭa}), with \emph{-ās} making an abstract noun out of the adjective: not the sweet thing, but the quality itself.

\hi{मिठाई}, which you met at the end of the welcome chapter, is the same stem with a different ending — the sweet you can hand someone. \hi{मिठास} is what is in it. One root, one for the tray and one for the taste.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fifth of five. That is what goes with thanks.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{miṭhās}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{miṭhās}, and \hi{मिठाई} beside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{मिठास} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sweetness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
